newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: BCCI liquidators in UAE processing requests.
newsitem.headline: BCCI liquidators in UAE processing requests.

text.p: The liquidation committee in charge of reimbursements for depositors in the UAE branches of the failed Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI) said on Tuesday it was actively processing their applications.

"The (UAE) Liquidation Administration...is actively processing the requests for payments of approved dividends in respect of deposits exceeding 20,000 dirhams ($5,450) for which the global liquidators are responsible to make the pro-rata payments," it said in a statement issued on Tuesday.
It said it was also handling "payments in full of deposits up to and including 20,000 dirhams which have been undertaken by the Central Bank of the UAE".
The statement was issued after small depositors complained that unlike larger depositors they had not received any reimbursement as promised by the UAE liquidation administrators in November.
"Please be advised that all such payments will be effected through the designated banks," the statement said.
It urged UAE depositors -- totalling 45,000 and owed nearly five billion dirhams -- who had not completed claims, to process their papers.

After a five-year struggle, BCCI liquidators in London said in early December that creditors of the bank would get payments of $2.65 billion, equal to 24.5 percent of their claims. Payment of another 10 percent of the admitted claims should be made 12 to 16 months later.

The UAE liquidation administrators said in November that UAE depositors of up to 20,000 dirhams on July 5, 1991, would be reimbursed fully by the UAE central bank as of mid-December, a move independent of the London liquidators.
"The decision to fully compensate small depositors is an initiative by the Abu Dhabi government which bears full responsibility for its financial repercussions," a source said.
Sources close to the UAE liquidators told Reuters on Tuesday the committee had delayed issuing cheques to the small depositors until it completed additional arrangements.
BCCI, founded in Luxembourg in 1972, was shut down in 1991 with debts of more than $12 billion after evidence emerged of widespread money laundering.

Liquidators of the failed bank said in May that an agreement with the majority shareholder, the Abu Dhabi government, was a key step towards paying the first dividend to about 250,000 creditors worldwide.
Under the agreement, Abu Dhabi, the biggest of seven emirates forming the UAE, paid $1.8 billion into a pool for distribution to creditors and depositors.
